nabob.etymology: Hind. nawab, from Ar. nawab, pl. of na\'8bb a vicegerent, governor. Cf Nawab.

nacre.etymology: F., cf. Sp. nácara, nácar, It. nacchera, naccaro, LL. nacara, nacrum; of Oriental origin, cf. Ar. nakir hollowed.

nadir.etymology: F., Sp., & It. nadir; all fr. Ar. nasiru's samt nadir, prop., the point opposite the zenith (as samt), in which nasir means alike, corresponding to. Cf. Azimuth, Zenith.

nag.etymology: OE. nagge, D. negge; akin to E. neigh.

naiad.etymology: L. naias, -adis, naïs, -idis, a water nymph, Gr naïade. Cf. Naid.

naive.etymology: F. naïf, fem. naïve, fr. L. nativus innate, natural, native. See Native, and cf. Naïf.

naivete.etymology: F. See Naïve, and cf. Nativity.

naked.etymology: AS. nacod; akin to D. naakt, G. nackt, OHG. nacchot, nahhot, Icel. nökvi, nakinn, Sw. naken, Dan. nögen, Goth. naqa, Lith. n, Russ. nagii, L. nudus, Skr. nagna. sq. root266. Cf. Nude.

name.etymology: AS. nama; akin to D. naam, OS. & OHG. namo, G. name, Icel. nafn, for namn, Dan. navn, Sw. namn, Goth. namo, L. nomen (perh. influenced by noscere, gnoscere, to learn to know), Gr. 'o`mona, Scr. naman. sq. root267. Cf. Anonymous, Ignominy, Misnomer, Nominal, Noun.

namesake.etymology: For name's sake; i. e., one named for the sake of another's name.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating an act, a process, the result of an act or a process, a state; also, a characteristic (as a theory, doctrine, idiom, etc.); as, baptism, galvanism, organism, hypnotism, socialism, sensualism, Anglicism.

nankeen.etymology: So called from its being originally manufactured at Nankin, in China.

nap.etymology: OE. nappen, AS. hn&ppian to take a nap, to slumber; cf. AS. hnipian to bend one's self, Icel. hnipna, hnipa, to droop.

nape.etymology: Perh. akin to knap a knop.

napery.etymology: OF. naperie, fr. nape a tablecloth, F. nappe, LL. napa, fr. L. mappa. See Map, and cf. Apron, Napkin.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

napkin.etymology: Dim. of OF. nape a tablecloth, cloth, F. nappe, L. mappa. See Napery.

narcissus.etymology: L. narcissus, and (personified) Narcissus, Gr. na`rkissos, Na`rkissos, fr. na`rkh torpor, in allusion to the narcotic properties of the flower. Cf. Narcotic.

narcosis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. na`rkwsis. See Narcotic.

narcotic.etymology: F. narcotique, Gr. na`rkh numbness, torpor.

nard.etymology: AS., fr. L. nardus, Gr. nêrd, Per. nard, Scr. nalada.

nargileh.etymology: Per. narghil, prop., a cocoanut; prob. so called because first made of a cocoanut.

narrate.etymology: L. narratus, p. p. of narrare to narrate, prob. for gnarigare, fr. gnarus knowing. See Ignore, Know.

narrow.etymology: OE. narwe, naru, AS. nearu; akin to OS. naru, naro.

narwhal.etymology: Sw. or Dan. narvhal; akin to Icel. nahvalr, and E. whale. the first syllable is perh. from Icel. nar corpse, dead body, in allusion to the whitish color its skin. See Whale.

nasal.etymology: F., from L. nasus the nose. See Nose.

nascent.etymology: L. nascens, -entis, p.pr. nasci to be born. See Nation, and cf. Naissant.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting pertaining to, or connected with, the nose; as, nasofrontal.

nasturtium.etymology: L. nasturtium, for nasitortium, fr. nasus nose + torquere, tortum, to twist, torture, in allusion to the causing one to make a wry face by its pungent taste. See Nose of the face, and Torture.

nasty.etymology: For older nasky; cf. dial. Sw. naskug, nasket.

natal.etymology: L. natalis, fr. natus, p.p. of nasci to be born: cf. F. natal. See Nation, and cf. Noel.

natation.etymology: L. natatio, fr. natare to swim: cf. F. natation. See Natant.

nation.etymology: F. nation, L. natio nation, race, orig., a being born, fr. natus, p.p. of nasci, to be born, for gnatus, gnaci, from the same root as E. kin. *44. See Kin kindred, and cf. Cognate, Natal, Native.

native.etymology: F. natif, L. nativus, fr. nasci, p.p. natus. See Nation, and cf. Naïve, Nelf a serf.

nativity.etymology: F. nativité, L. nativitas. See Native, and cf. NaïvetÉ.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

natural.etymology: OE. naturel, F. naturel, fr. L. naturalis, fr. natura. See Nature.

nature.etymology: F., fr. L. natura, fr. natus born, produced, p.p. of nasci to be born. See Nation.

naught.etymology: OE. naught, nought, naht, nawiht, AS. n, n, n; ne not + wiht thing, whit; hence, not ever a whit. See No, adv. Whit, and cf. Aught, Not.

nausea.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Nave of a church, and cf. Noise.

nauseate.etymology: L. nauseare, nauseatum, fr. nausea. See Nausea.

nautch.etymology: Hind. nach, fr. Skr. n dance.

nautical.etymology: L. nauticus, Gr. nautique. See Nave of a church.

nautilus.etymology: L., fr. gr. Nave of a church.

naval.etymology: L. navalis, fr. navis ship: cf. F. naval. See Nave of a church.

nave.etymology: AS. nafu; akin to D. naaf, G. nabe, OHG. naba, Icel. nöf, Dan. nav, Sw. naf, Skr. nabhi nave and navel: cf. L. umbo boss of a shield. *260. Cf. Navel.

navel.etymology: AS. nafela, fr. nafu nave; akin to D. navel, G. nabel, OHG. nabolo, Icel. nafli, Dan. navle, Sw. nafle, L. umbilicus, Gr. n. *260. See Nave hub, and cf. Omphalic, Nombril, Umbilical.

navicular.etymology: L. navicularius, fr. navicula, dim. of navis ship: cf. F. naviculaire.

navigable.etymology: L. navigabilis: cf. F. navigable. See Navigate.

navigate.etymology: L. navigatus, p.p. of navigare, v.t. & i.; navis ship + agere to move, direct. See Nave, and Agent.

navy.etymology: OF. navie, fr. L. navis ship. See Nave of a church.

nay.etymology: Icel. nei; akin to E. no. See No, adv.

near.etymology: AS. neár, compar. of neáh nigh. See Nigh.

neat.etymology: AS. neát; akin to OHG. n, Icel. naut, Sw. nöt, Dan. nöd, and to AS. neótan to make use of, G. geniessen, Goth. niutan to have a share in, have joy of, Lith. nauda use, profit.

neb.etymology: AS. nebb head, face; akin to D. neb, Icel. nef, beak of a bird, nose, Dan. næb beak, bill, Sw. näbb, näf, and prob. also to D. sneb, snavel, bill, beak, G. schnabel, Dan. & Sw. snabel, and E. snap. Cf. Nib, Snap, Snaffle.

nebula.etymology: L., mist, cloud; akin to Gr. nebel mist, OHG. nebul, D. nevel, Skr. nabhas cloud, mist. Cf. Nebule.

nebulous.etymology: L. nebulosus: cf. F. nébuleux. See Nebula.

necessary.etymology: From Middle English necessarye , from Old French necessaire , from Latin necessārius ( “ unavoidable , inevitable , required ” ) , variant of necesse ( “ unavoidable , inevitable ” ) , probably from ne or non cessum , from the perfect passive participle of cēdō ( “ yield ; avoid , withdraw ” ) ; see cede .

necessitate.etymology: Cf. L. necessitatus, p.p. of necessitare, and F. nécessiter. See Necessity.

necessity.etymology: OE. necessite, F. nécessité, L. necessitas, fr. necesse. See Necessary.

neck.etymology: OE. necke, AS. hnecca; akin to D. nek the nape of the neck, G. nacken, OHG. nacch, hnacch, Icel. hnakki, Sw. nacke, Dan. nakke.

necrology.etymology: Gr. -logy: cf. F. nécrologie. See Necromancy.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

necromancy.etymology: OE. nigromaunce, nigromancie, OF. nigromance, F. nécromance, nécromancie, from L. necromantia, Gr. necare to kill, Skr. na() to perish, vanish) + mania. See Mania, and cf. Internecine, Noxious. The old spelling is due to confusion with L. niger black. Hence the name black art.

nectariferous.etymology: L. nectar nectar + -ferous: cf. F. nectarifère.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

nee.etymology: F., fr. L. nata, fem. of natus, p.p. of nasci to be born. See Nation.

need.etymology: OE. need, neod, nede, AS. neád, nyd; akin to D. nood, G. not, noth, Icel. nauedhr, Sw. & Dan. nöd, Goth. naups.

needle.etymology: OE. nedle, AS. n; akin to D. neald, OS. nadla, G. nadel, OHG. nadal, nadala, Icel. nal, Sw. nål, Dan. naal, and also to G. nähen to sew, OHG. najan, L. nere to spin, Gr. snare: cf. Gael. & Ir. snathad needle, Gael. snath thread, G. schnur string, cord.

needs.etymology: Orig. gen. of need, used as an adverb. Cf. - wards.

nefarious.etymology: L. nefarius, fr. nefas crime, wrong; ne not + fas divine law; akin to fari to speak. See No, adv., and Fate.

negation.etymology: L. negatio, fr. negare to say no, to deny; ne not + the root of aio I say; cf. Gr. ah to say; cf. F. négation. See No, adv., and cf. Adage, Deny, Renegade.

negative.etymology: F. négatif, L. negativus, fr. negare to deny. See Negation.

neglect.etymology: L. neglectus, p.p. of neglegere (negligere) to disregard, neglect, the literal sense prob. neing, not to pick up; nec not, nor (fr. ne not + -que, a particle akin to Goth. -h, -uh, and prob. to E. who; cf. Goth. nih nor) + L. legere to pick up, gather. See No, adv., Legend, Who.

negligee.etymology: F. négligé, fr. négliger to neglect, L. negligere. See Neglect.

negligent.etymology: F. négligent, L. negligens,p.pr. of negligere. See Neglect.

negotiant.etymology: L. negotians, prop. p.pr. of negotiari: cf. F. négociant.

negotiate.etymology: L. negotiatus, p.p. of negotiari, fr. negotium business; nec not + otium leisure. Cf. Neglect.

negress.etymology: Cf. F. négrese, fem. of négre a negro. See Negro.

negro.etymology: Sp. or Pg. negro, fr. negro black, L. niger; perh. akin to E. night.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

neigh.etymology: OE. neien, AS. hn, prob. of imitative origin; cf. MHG. n, Icel. hneggja, gneggja, Sw. gnägga. Cf. Nag a horse.

neighbor.etymology: OE. neighebour, AS. neáhgeb; neáh nigh + gebr a dweller, farmer; akin to D. nabuur, G. nachbar, OHG. nahgib. See Nigh, and Boor.

neither.etymology: OE. neiter, nother, nouther, AS. naw, nahwæ; na never, not + hwæ whether. The word has followed the form of either. See No, and Whether, and cf. Neuter, Nor.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning new, recent, late; and in chemistry designating specifically that variety of metameric hydrocarbons which, when the name was applied, had been recently classified, and in which at least one carbon atom in connected directly with four other carbon atoms; -- contrasted with normal and iso-; as, neopentane; the neoparaffins. Also used adjectively.

A prefix meaning new, recent, late; and in chemistry designating specifically that variety of metameric hydrocarbons which, when the name was applied, had been recently classified, and in which at least one carbon atom in connected directly with four other carbon atoms; -- contrasted with normal and iso-; as, neopentane; the neoparaffins. Also used adjectively.
Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

A suffix, denoting that the element indicated enters into certain compounds with its highest valence, or with a valence relatively higher than in compounds where the name of the element ends in -ous; as, ferric, sulphuric. It is also used in the general sense of pertaining to; as, hydric, sodic, calcic.

A prefix meaning new, recent, late; and in chemistry designating specifically that variety of metameric hydrocarbons which, when the name was applied, had been recently classified, and in which at least one carbon atom in connected directly with four other carbon atoms; -- contrasted with normal and iso-; as, neopentane; the neoparaffins. Also used adjectively.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

neophyte.etymology: L. neophytis, Gr. néophyte. See New, and Be.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning new, recent, late; and in chemistry designating specifically that variety of metameric hydrocarbons which, when the name was applied, had been recently classified, and in which at least one carbon atom in connected directly with four other carbon atoms; -- contrasted with normal and iso-; as, neopentane; the neoparaffins. Also used adjectively.

nephew.etymology: OE. neveu, nevou, nevu, fr. F. neveu, OF. also, nevou, L. nepos; akin to AS. nefa, D. neef, G. neffe, OHG. nevo, Icel. nefi a kinsman, gr. nepat grandson, descendant. sq. root262. Cf. Niece, Nepotism.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

nephritic.etymology: L. nephriticus, gr. néphrétique. See Nephritis.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

nepotism.etymology: L. nepus, nepotus, nephew: cf. F. népotisme. See Nephew.

nerve.etymology: OE. nerfe, F. nerf, L. nervus, akin to Gr. needle. Cf. Neuralgia.

nervous.etymology: L. nervosus sinewy, vigorous: cf. F. nerveux. See Nerve.

nescience.etymology: L. nescientia, fr. nesciens, p.pr. of nescire not to know; ne not + scire to know.

ness.etymology: AS. næs, ns; akin to Icel. nes, Sw. näs, Dan. næs, and E. nose. sq. root 261. See Nose.

nest.etymology: AS. nest; akin to D. & G. nest, Sw. näste, L. nidus, for nisdus, Skr. ni resting place, nest; cf. Lith. lizdas, Arm. neiz, Gael. & Ir. nead. Prob. from the particle ni down, Skr. ni + the root of E. sit, and thus orig., a place to sit down in. sq. root 264. See Nether, and Sit, and cf. Eyas, Nidification, Nye.

net.etymology: AS. net; akin to D. net, OS. net, netti, OHG. nezzi, G. netz, Icel. & Dan. net, Sw. nät, Goth. nati; of uncertain origin.

nether.etymology: OE. nethere, neithere, AS. ni, fr. the adv. ni downward; akin to neo below, beneath, D. neder down, G. nieder, Sw. nedre below, nether, a. & adv., and also to Skr. ni down. sq. root201. Cf. Beneath.

nettle.etymology: AS. netele; akin to D. netel, G. nessel, OHG. nezzïla, nazza, Dan. nelde, nälde, Sw. nässla; cf, Lith. notere.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
A combining denoting a nerve, of or pertaining to a nerve or the nervous system.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A combining denoting a nerve, of or pertaining to a nerve or the nervous system.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.
A combining denoting a nerve, of or pertaining to a nerve or the nervous system.

neuter.etymology: L., fr. ne not + uter whether; akin to E. whether. See No, and Whether, and cf. Neither.

neutral.etymology: L. neutralis, fr. neuter. See Neuter.

never.etymology: AS. n; ne not, no + ever.

nevertheless.etymology: Never + the (see The by that) + less.

new.etymology: OE. OE. newe, AS. niwe, neowe; akin to D. nieuw, OS. niwi, OHG. niuwi, G. neu, Icel. n, Dan. & Sw. ny, Goth. niujis, Lith. naujas, Russ. novuii, Ir. nua, nuadh, Gael. nuadh, W. newydd, Armor. nevez, L. novus, gr. nava, and prob. to E. now. Now, and cf. Announce, Innovate, Neophyte, Novel.

newt.etymology: OE. ewt, evete, AS. efete, with n prefixed, an ewt being understood as a newt. Cf. Eft.

next.etymology: AS. n, niéhst, n, superl. of neáh nigh. See Nigh.

nice.etymology: OE., foolish, fr. OF. nice ignorant, fool, fr. L. nescius ignorant; ne not + scius knowing, scire to know. perhaps influenced by E. nesh delicate, soft. See No, and Science.

niche.etymology: F., fr. It. nicchia, prop., a shell-like recess in a wall, fr. nicchio a shellfish, mussel, fr. L. mytilus.

nick.etymology: AS. nicor a marine monster; akin to D. nikker a water spite, Icel. nykr, ONG. nihhus a crocodile, G. nix a water sprite; cf. Gr. nij. Cf. Nix.

nickel.etymology: G., fr. Sw. nickel, abbrev. from Sw. kopparnickel copper-nickel, a name given in derision, as it was thought to be a base ore of copper. The origin of the second part of the word is uncertain. Cf. Kupfer-nickel, Copper-nickel.

nickname.etymology: OE. ekename surname, hence, a nickname, an ekename being understood as a nekename, influenced also by E. nick, v. See Eke, and Name.

nictate.etymology: L. nictare, nictatum, from nicere to beckon.

niece.etymology: OE. nece, F. nièce, LL. neptia, for L. neptis a granddaughter, niece, akin to nepos. See Nephew.

niggard.etymology: Icel. hnöggr niggardly, stingy + -ard; cf. Sw. njugg, AS. hneáw.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

niggle.etymology: Dim. of Prov. E. nig to clip money; cf. also Prov. E. nig a small piece.

nigh.etymology: OE. nigh, neigh, neih, AS. neáh, n; akin to D. na, adv., OS. nah, a., OHG. nah, G. nah, a., nach to, after, Icel. na (in comp.) nigh, Goth. n, n, adv., nigh. Cf. Near, Neighbor, Next.

night.etymology: OE. night, niht, AS. neaht, niht; akin to D. nacht, OS. & OHG. naht, G. nacht, Icel. n, Sw. natt, Dan. nat, Goth. nachts, Lith. naktis, Russ. noche, W. nos, Ir. nochd, L. nox, noctis, gr. nakta, nakti. sq. root 265. Cf. Equinox, Nocturnal.

nightingale.etymology: OE. nihtegale,nightingale, AS. nihtegale; niht night + galan to sing, akin to E. yell; cf. D. nachtegaal, OS. nahtigala, OHG. nahtigala, G. nachtigall, Sw. näktergal, Dan. nattergal. See Night, and Yell.

nightmare.etymology: Night + mare incubus. See Mare incubus.

nihilism.etymology: L. nihil nothing: cf. F. nihilisme. See Annihilate.

nilotic.etymology: L. Niloticus, fr. Nilus th Nile, Gr. nilotique.

nim.etymology: AS. niman. sq. root 7. Cf. Nimble.

nimble.etymology: OE. nimel, prob. orig., quick at seizing, fr. nimen to take, AS. niman; akin to D. nemen, G. nehmen, OHG. neman, Icel. nema, Goth. nima, and prob. to Gr. Nomand, Numb.

nimbus.etymology: L., a rain storm, a rain cloud, the cloudshaped which enveloped the gods when they appeared on earth.

nimiety.etymology: L. nimietas, fr. nimius, a., nimis, adv., too much.

nine.etymology: OE. nine, nihen, AS. nigon, nigan; akin to D. & LG. negen, OS. & OFries. nigun, OHG. niun, G. neun, Icel. niu, sw. nio, Dan. ni, Goth. niun, Ir. & Gael. naoi, W. naw, L. novem, gr. navan; of unknown origin. Novembeer.

nineteen.etymology: AS. nigont, nigont. See Nine, and Ten.

ninny.etymology: Cf. It. ninno, ninna, a baby, Sp. niño, niña, child, infant, It. ninna, ninna nanna, lullably, prob. fr. ni, na, as used in singing a child to sleep.

nip.etymology: LG. & D. nippen to sip; akin to Dan. nippe, G. nippen.

nipple.etymology: Formerly neble, a dim. of neb. See Neb, Nib.

nisus.etymology: L., fr. niti, p.p. nisus, to strive.

nit.etymology: AS. hnitu; akin to D. neet, G. niss, OHG. niz; cf. gr. gnit, Sw. gnet, Dan. gnid, Russ. & Pol. gnida, Bohem. hnida, W. nedd.

niter.etymology: F. nitre, L. nitrum native soda, natron, Gr. nit, natr natron. Cf. Natron.

nitid.etymology: L. nitidus, fr. nitere. See 3d Neat.

nitre.etymology: F. nitre, L. nitrum native soda, natron, Gr. nit, natr natron. Cf. Natron.

nitrify.etymology: Niter + -fy: cf. F. nitrifer. See Niter.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

A combining form (used also adjectively) designating certain compounds of nitrogen or of its acids, as nitrohydrochloric, nitrocalcite; also, designating the group or radical NO2, or its compounds, as nitrobenzene. Nitro group, the radical NO2; -- called also nitroxyl.

A combining form (used also adjectively) designating certain compounds of nitrogen or of its acids, as nitrohydrochloric, nitrocalcite; also, designating the group or radical NO2, or its compounds, as nitrobenzene. Nitro group, the radical NO2; -- called also nitroxyl.

A combining form (used also adjectively) designating certain compounds of nitrogen or of its acids, as nitrohydrochloric, nitrocalcite; also, designating the group or radical NO2, or its compounds, as nitrobenzene. Nitro group, the radical NO2; -- called also nitroxyl.

A combining form (used also adjectively) designating certain compounds of nitrogen or of its acids, as nitrohydrochloric, nitrocalcite; also, designating the group or radical NO2, or its compounds, as nitrobenzene. Nitro group, the radical NO2; -- called also nitroxyl.

nitrogen.etymology: L. nitrum natron + -gen: cf. F. nitrogène. See Niter.

roots.meaning: A combining form (used also adjectively) designating certain compounds of nitrogen or of its acids, as nitrohydrochloric, nitrocalcite; also, designating the group or radical NO2, or its compounds, as nitrobenzene. Nitro group, the radical NO2; -- called also nitroxyl.

nitrous.etymology: L. nitrosus full of natron: cf. F. nitreux. See Niter.

nivose.etymology: F., fr. L. nix. nivis, snow.

nobility.etymology: L. nobilitas: cf. OF. nobilité. See Noble.

noble.etymology: F. noble, fr. L. nobilis that can be or is known, well known, famous, highborn, noble, fr.noscere to know. See know.

nocent.etymology: L. nocens, p.pr. of nocere to hurt. See Nuisance, Noxious.

noctambulation.etymology: L. nox, noctis, night + ambulare to walk: cf. F. noctambulation.

noctiluca.etymology: L. noctiluca something that shines by night, fr. nox, noctis, night + lucere to shine, lux light.

nocturnal.etymology: L. nocturnalis, nocturnus, fr. nox, noctis, night. See Night, and cf. Nocturn.

nod.etymology: OE. nodden; cf. OHG. kn, genuot, to shake, and E. nudge.

noddle.etymology: OE. nodil, nodle; perh. fr. nod, because the head is the nodding part of the body, or perh. akin to E. knot; cf. Prov. E. nod the nape of the neck.

node.etymology: L. nodus; perh. akin to E. knot. Cf. Noose, Nowed.

nodule.etymology: L. nodulus, dim. of nodus knot: cf. F. nodule.

noel.etymology: F. noël, L. natalis birthday, fr. natalis natal. See Natal.

noggin.etymology: Ir. noigin, or Gael. noigean. Cf. lst Nog.

noise.etymology: F. noise noisy strife, quarrel, brawl, fr. L. nausea seasickness, sickness, disgust. See Nausea.

noisome.etymology: For noysome, fr. noy for annoy. See Annoy.

nomad.etymology: L. nomas, -adis, Gr. niman to take, and E. nimble: cf. F. nomade. Cf. Astronomy, Economy, Nimble, Nemesis, Numb, Number.

nombril.etymology: F. nombril, for OF. lombril, i. e., ombril, with the article, a dim. fr. L. umbilicus the navel. See Navel.

nomenclature.etymology: L. nomenclatura: cf. F. nomenclature. See Nomenclator.

nominal.etymology: L. nominalis, fr. nomen, nominis, name. See Name.

nominate.etymology: L. nominatus, p. p. of nominare to nominate, fr. nomen name. See Name.

nominative.etymology: L. nominativus belonging to a name, nominative.

roots.meaning: A suffix used, chiefly in law terms, in a passive signification, to indicate the direct or indirect object of an action, or the one to whom an act is done or on whom a right is conferred; as in assignee, donee, alienee, grantee, etc. It is correlative to -or, the agent or doer.

nonage.etymology: LL. nonagium, from L. nonus ninth, novem nine.

nonagenarian.etymology: L. nonagenarius containing, or consisting of, ninety, fr. nonageni ninety each; akin to novem nine.

nonce.etymology: For the nonce, OE. for the nones, a corruption of for then ones, where n. in then is a relic of AS. m in , dat. of the article and demonstrative pronoun, E. the. See For, Once, and The.

nonchalant.etymology: F., fr. non not (L. non) + chaloir to concern one's self for, fr. L. calere to be warm, to be inflamed with desire, to be troubled. See Non-, and Caldron.

roots.meaning: A prefix used in the sense of not; un-; in-; as in nonattention, or non-attention, nonconformity, nonmetallic, nonsuit.
A prefix used in the sense of not; un-; in-; as in nonattention, or non-attention, nonconformity, nonmetallic, nonsuit.

none.etymology: OE. none, non, nan, no, na, AS. nan, fr. ne not + an one. No, a. & adv., One, and cf. Non-, Null, a.

roots.meaning: A prefix used in the sense of not; un-; in-; as in nonattention, or non-attention, nonconformity, nonmetallic, nonsuit.

nones.etymology: L. nonae, so called because it was the ninth day before the ides, fr. nonus ninth, from novem nine. See Nine, Nones, 2, Noon .

nonplus.etymology: L. non not + plus more, further. See Plural.

nonsense.etymology: Pref. non- + sense: cf. F. nonsens.

roots.meaning: A prefix used in the sense of not; un-; in-; as in nonattention, or non-attention, nonconformity, nonmetallic, nonsuit.

nook.etymology: OE. nok; cf. Gael. & Ir. niuc.

noon.etymology: AS. n, orig., the ninth hour, fr. L.nona (sc. hora) the ninth hour, then applied to the church services (called nones) at that hour, the time of which was afterwards changed to noon. See Nine, and cf. Nones, Nunchion.

noontide.etymology: From noon + tide time; cf. AS. n the ninth hour.

noose.etymology: Prob. fr. OF. nous, nom. sing. or acc. pl. of nou knot, F. n, L. nodus. Cf. Node.

norm.etymology: L. norma a rule. See Normal, a.

normal.etymology: L. normalis, fr. norma rule, pattern, carpenter's square; prob. akin to noscere to know; cf. Gr. normal. See Known, and cf. Abnormal, Enormous.

norse.etymology: Dan. Norsk, fr. nord north. See North.

north.etymology: AS. noredh; akin to D. noord, G., Sw., & Dan. nord, Icel. noredhr. Cf. Norman, Norse.

northman.etymology: AS. noredhman. See North, and Man, and cf. Norman.

norwegian.etymology: Cf. Icel. Noregr, Norvegr, Norway. See North, and Way.

nose.etymology: AS. nosu; akin to D. neus, G. nase, OHG. nasa, Icel. nös, Sw. näsa, Dan. näse, Lith. nosis, Russ. nos', L. nasus, nares, Skr. nasa, nas. Nasal, Nasturtium, Naze, Nostril, Nozzle.

nosegay.etymology: Nose + gay in the sense of a gay or showy thing.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

nostril.etymology: OE. nosethril, nosethirl, AS. nospyrl; nos for nosu nose + pyrel opening, hole, from pyrel pierced, for pyrhel, fr. purh through. Nose, and Through, and cf. Thrill.

nostrum.etymology: Neut. sing. of L. noster ours, fr. nos we. See Us.

not.etymology: Contr. from ne wot. See 2d Note.

notable.etymology: F. notable, L. notabilis, fr. notare to mark, nota mark, note. See 5th Note.

notary.etymology: F. notaire, L. notarius notary (in sense 1), fr. nota mark. See 5th Note.

notate.etymology: L. notatus marked, p. p. of notare to mark. See 5th Note.

notation.etymology: L. notatio a marking, observing, etymology, fr. notare to mark, nota a mark: cf. F. notation. See 5th Note.

notch.etymology: Akin to nock; cf. OD. nock, OSw. nocka. Cf. Nick a notch.

note.etymology: AS. hnitan to strike against, imp. hnat.

notice.etymology: F., fr. L. notitia a being known, knowledge, fr. noscere, notum, to know. See Know.

notify.etymology: F. notifier, L. notificare; notus known (p. p. of noscere to known) + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Know, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

notion.etymology: L. notio, fr. noscere to know: cf. F. notion. See Know.

notorious.etymology: L. notorius pointing out, making known, fr. noscere, notum, to known: cf. F. notoire. See Know.

notwithstanding.etymology: Originally the participle of withstand, with not prefixed.

noun.etymology: OF. noun, nun, num, non, nom, F. nom, fr. L. nomen name. See Name.

nourish.etymology: OE. norisen, norischen, OF. nurir, nurrir, norir, F. norrir, fr. L. nutrire. Cf. Nurse, Nutriment, and see -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

nova.etymology: L., fem. sing. of novus new.

novation.etymology: L. novatio; novus new: cf. F. novation.

novel.etymology: OF. novel, nuvel, F. nouvel, nouveau, L. novellus, dim. of novus new. See New.

novelette.etymology: Dim. of novel, n. See Novel.

novelty.etymology: OF. novelté, F. nouveauté, L. novellitas.

november.etymology: L. November, or Novembris (sc. mensis), the ninth month of the old Roman year, which began with March, fr. novem nine: cf. F. Novembre. See Nine.

novice.etymology: F., from L. novicius, novitius, new, from novus new. See New, and cf. Novitious.

now.etymology: OE. nou, nu, AS. nu, nu; akin to D., OS., & OHG. nu, G. nu, nun, Icel., nu, Dan., Sw., & Goth. nu, L. nunc, Gr. nu, nu. *193. Cf. New.

nowadays.etymology: For now on (OE. an) days. See A-, 1.

nowhere.etymology: AS. nahwær. See No, and Where.

nowise.etymology: For in no wise. See Wise, n.

noxious.etymology: L. noxius, fr. noxa harm; akin to nocere to harm, hurt. Cf. Nuisance, Necromancy.

nozzle.etymology: A dim. of nose. sq. root261

nubble.etymology: Cf. LG. nubben to knock, cuff.

nubile.etymology: L. nubilis, fr. nubere to marry: cf. F. nubile. See Nuptial.

nucellus.etymology: NL., dim. of nux, nucis, a nut.

nucleolus.etymology: L., a little nut, dim. of nucleus.

nucleus.etymology: L., a kernel, dim. fr. nux, nucis, nut. Cf. Newel post.

nudge.etymology: Cf. Prov. G. knütschen to squeeze, pinch, E. Knock.

nugatory.etymology: L. nugatorius, fr. nugari to trifle, nugae jests, trifles.

nugget.etymology: Earlier niggot, prob. for nigot, an ingot. See Ingot.

nuisance.etymology: OE. noisance, OF. noisance, nuisance, fr. L. nocentia guilt, fr. nocere to hurt, harm; akin to necare to kill. Cf Necromancy, Nocent, Noxious, Pernicious.

null.etymology: L. nullus not any, none; ne not + ullus any, a dim. of unus one; cf. F. nul. See No, and One, and cf. None.

nullify.etymology: L. nullificare; nullus none + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Null, a., and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

nullity.etymology: LL. nullitias, fr. L. nullus none: cf. F. nullité . See Null.

numb.etymology: OE. nume, nome, prop., seized, taken, p. p. of nimen to take, AS. niman, p. p. numen. *7. See Nimble, Nomad, and cf. Benumb.

number.etymology: OE. nombre, F. nombre, L. numerus; akin to Gr. Numb, Nomad, and cf. Numerate, Numero, Numerous.

numerable.etymology: L. numerabilis. See Number, v. t.

numeral.etymology: L. numeralis, fr. numerus number: cf. F. numéral. See Number, n.

numerate.etymology: L. numeratus, p. p. of numerare to count. See Number, v.

numeration.etymology: L. numeratio a counting out: cf. F. numération.

numeric.etymology: Cf. F. numérique. See Number, n.

numerical.etymology: Cf. F. numérique. See Number, n.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

nummulite.etymology: L. nummus a coin + -lite: cf. F. nummulite.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

nun.etymology: OE. nunne, AS. nunne, fr. L. nonna nun, nonnus monk; cf. Gr. Nunnery.

nuncio.etymology: It. nunzio, nuncio, fr. L. nuncius, nuntius, messenger; perh. akin to novus new, E. new, and thus, one who brings news. Cf. Announce.

nunnery.etymology: OE. nonnerie, OF. nonerie, F. nonnerie, fr. nonne nun, L. nonna. See Nun.

nuptial.etymology: L. nuptialis, fr. nuptiae marriage, wedding, fr. nubere, nuptum, prop., to cover, to veil, hence, to marry, as the head of the bride was covered with a veil; cf. Gr. nuptial.

nurse.etymology: OE. nourse, nurice, norice, OF. nurrice, norrice, nourrice, F. nourrice, fr. L. nutricia nurse, prop., fem. of nutricius that nourishes; akin to nutrix, -icis, nurse, fr. nutrire to nourish. See Nourish, and cf. Nutritious.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

nurture.etymology: OE. norture, noriture, OF. norriture, norreture, F. nourriture, fr. L. nutritura a nursing, suckling. See Nourish.

nut.etymology: OE. nute, note, AS. hnutu; akin to D. noot, G. nuss, OHG. nuz, Icel. hnot, Sw. nöt, Dan. nöd.

nutation.etymology: L. nutatio a nodding, fr. nutare to nod: cf. F. nutation.

nutmeg.etymology: OE. notemuge; note nut + OF. muge musk, of the same origin as E. musk; cf. OF. noix muguette nutmeg, F. noix muscade. See Nut, and Musk.

nutria.etymology: Sp. nutria an otter, fr. L. lutra, lytra.

nutrient.etymology: L. nutriens, p. pr. of nutrire. See Nourish.

nutriment.etymology: L. nutrimentum, fr. nutrire to nourish. See Nourish.

nutritious.etymology: L. nutricius, nutritius, from nutrix, -icis, a nurse, nutrire to nourish. See Nurse, Nourish.

nylghau.etymology: Hind. & Per. nilgaw, prop., a blue cow; Per. nil blue + gaw cow. See Lilac, and Cow the animal.

nymph.etymology: L. nympha nymph, bride, young woman, Gr. nymphe. Cf. Nuptial.
